name: Photonic Approach
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Computing With Particles of Light
lesson.summary: Photonic quantum computers encode information in particles of light that barely interact with their surroundings, trading easy isolation for gates that are hard to build at all.
lesson.body:
Every other qubit technology in this chapter starts from the same basic problem: matter interacts with its environment, and that interaction destroys quantum information. The photonic approach tries to sidestep the problem entirely by using something that barely interacts with anything, a single particle of light. A photon can travel down an optical fiber or through free space for enormous distances while retaining its quantum state, encoded in a property like polarization, the timing of its arrival, or, in continuous variable schemes, properties of squeezed light. Because photons carry no charge and rarely collide with stray matter, they largely avoid the thermal noise that forces superconducting circuits into a refrigerator.

That is the appeal, and it is a real one: photonic systems can run near room temperature, without the dilution refrigerators that dominate the cost and footprint of superconducting labs, and they are the natural medium for connecting separate quantum computers into a network, since photons are already how signals travel down fiber optic cables. PsiQuantum is betting on standard photonic components and integrated silicon chips to build systems this way, while Xanadu has pursued continuous variable photonic qubits, demonstrating a device called Borealis using over two hundred modes of squeezed light.

But the reality that qubits are extremely fragile does not disappear here, it just changes shape. Photons are hard to store: there is no simple photonic equivalent of parking a qubit in memory while you work on another one, because a stationary photon is close to a contradiction in terms. Photon loss, absorption or scattering somewhere along the optical path, is the dominant error mechanism, and every mirror, beam splitter, and fiber junction is another chance to lose the particle carrying your information entirely. Detectors are also imperfect, sometimes missing a photon that arrived or registering one that did not.

The harder problem is making two photons interact at all. Two qubit gates in most other platforms rely on some direct physical interaction: a shared electromagnetic field, a laser coupled vibration, a blockade effect. Photons famously do not interact with each other in ordinary optical materials, so builders either rely on measurement based schemes that make gates probabilistic, succeeding only some fraction of the time and requiring redundant attempts to guarantee success, or they use exotic nonlinear materials whose useful effects are extremely weak. This is why photonic quantum computing has leaned so heavily on narrow demonstrations such as Gaussian boson sampling, including the Jiuzhang experiments from a research group in China, rather than general purpose programmable circuits.

The honest summary is a genuine tradeoff rather than a free lunch: photonic qubits solve the isolation half of fragility remarkably well, at the cost of making the interaction half, the very thing a computer needs to do useful work, unusually difficult to engineer.
